findings.reason: the rule removes the stop without removing the penalty the plan's own §1 question 1 asks about ("does anything stop, cut short or penalise a run when it passes its deadline?"), so a worker obeying §3 is still recorded as an overrun and Jev keeps seeing the node as one.
findings.text: §3 permits a worker to keep running past its deadline (launch plus budget times `fences.budget_grace_multiple`) to finish a named bounded step, but the run is still classified `budget_overrun` by `_budget_timing`/`_apply_budget_watchdog` (`reckon/crew/recovery_stream.py:236`, which sets `budget_overrun` from elapsed > budget regardless of watchdog enforcement) and surfaced through the picker's budget metrics (`reckon/crew/query.py:65-68`)

findings.reason: §3 is implementable and §2 deferred, so §2 can be built without §3's hard stop in place and neither section declares how the two deadlines compose.
findings.text: the `plan-section-depends-on` entry for s2 is `[s1]` only, but §2's gate-verb shape (line 65) states the deadline as launch plus budget plus gate time by rewriting `time_fence_statement`, the same function and prompt sentences §3 rewrites

findings.reason: the section's whole motivation rests on counts no reader can check, and the precedent in this plan is to name the queried set beside the number.
findings.text: the Why attributes "163 of its 337 worker ledger rows as resumes" and "19 of 755 recent worker manifests that name a deadline stop" to an unnamed session with no run id, ledger query or manifest set a reader can open, the same defect an earlier review raised against §1's 75-of-104 cutoff and the author fixed by recording ids

response_events.reason: nothing that reads an overrun penalises it: budget_overrun is the token verdict (recovery_stream.py:236), a wall overrun sets ceiling_overrun and budget_overrun_seconds, and their only readers are the overrun-cause label (recovery_stream.py:165) and the crew runs view (crew_run_commands.py:269-278); the picker package reads no overrun field (grep over reckon/crew/picker/ returns nothing), and the opt-in watchdog acts at budget times the grace multiple, the same instant as the hard stop. A run that finishes a named step past its deadline did take longer than its budget, so recording that is a true sizing fact, not a penalty

rubric_items.anchors_resolve: a finding — the two counts that motivate s3 ("163 of 337 worker ledger rows as resumes", "19 of 755 recent worker manifests") name no run, log, manifest set or query a reader can open.
rubric_items.done_when: pass — each implementable node's done-when names a declared negative control (s3 mutates `compose_prompt` and the resumed-attempt call; §1's scanners are checked against known positives).
rubric_items.evidence_paths: pass — s3's gate arms write under the run directory, and its cited anchors (`prompts.py`, `recovery_stream.py`, `dispatch_sessions.py`, `worker-protocol.md`) are repository paths, not scratchpads.
rubric_items.naming: pass — `tests/test_a_deadline_lets_a_named_batch_finish.py` and the restated rule carry no plan label, stage name, ticket number or version tag, and no changelog prose.
rubric_items.reasoning: a finding — s3 lets a worker run past its deadline to the hard stop, but nothing in the section addresses the `budget_overrun` accounting that still records and penalises exactly that run.
rubric_items.single_goal: pass — s3 carries one deliverable, the one deadline rule restated at every place a worker is told it.
rubric_items.wiring: a finding — s3 is declared implementable and depends on nothing, but §2's only declared dependency is s1 even though §2's gate-verb shape rewrites the same `time_fence_statement` and stop instruction that §3 rewrites.
